title: Tres leches cake
subtitle: Mexican milk-soaked sponge with whipped cream topping
excerpt: Tres leches cake is a Mexican sponge soaked in a mixture of three milks: evaporated milk, condensed milk, and double cream. The sponge absorbs the milks to become extraordinarily moist and custardy, while the top is finished with softly whipped cream. The sponge must be completely cool before soaking, and the cake needs at least four hours in the refrigerator for full absorption.
sourceNotes: Traditional Mexican and Latin American recipe (public domain culinary tradition). Documented in various 20th-century Mexican cookbooks (public domain). Nestlé recipe variations widely documented as public-domain adaptations.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made the day before serving: soak the cooled sponge, cover, and refrigerate overnight.

baking.decoratingTechnique: Softly whipped cream spread over top; cinnamon or fruit to finish

recipeTools.notes: 30 x 20 cm tin, greased and lined.
For beating egg whites and yolks.

glossaryTerms.definition: A gentle mixing technique used to combine a light, airy mixture (such as beaten egg whites) with a heavier one without deflating it. A large spatula or metal spoon is drawn down through the centre of the bowl and swept up the side in a single motion, rotating the bowl a quarter turn between strokes. Stirring or beating instead of folding collapses the air bubbles and produces a dense result.

Eggs with the yolk and white divided into separate bowls before use. The yolks add richness and colour; the whites, when beaten to stiff peaks, add lift and lightness. For tres leches, the yolks are beaten with sugar to a thick pale ribbon, the whites are beaten separately, and both are folded into the flour to give a light, absorbent sponge that can hold the three-milk soak without becoming sodden.

Beating cream rapidly to incorporate air until it thickens. Soft peaks hold a shape but the tip droops when the whisk is lifted; firm peaks stand straight. Tres leches is topped with soft-peak cream, which is spreadable and slightly yielding. Continue beating past soft peaks and the cream becomes stiff and eventually grainy; there is no reliable recovery from over-whipped cream.

content.text: Tres leches cake starts with
separated eggs
beaten independently and
folding
together to make a light sponge designed to absorb liquid. You get a deeply moist, custardy cake that slices cleanly and holds up well in the refrigerator. The
whipping
of the cream for the topping needs to stop at soft peaks; the cake is already very rich and the topping should be light rather than stiff.
Method
Bake the sponge
Heat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius (conventional). Grease and line a 30 x 20 cm rectangular baking tin.

Beat the egg yolks with three-quarters of the caster sugar (about 115 g) and the vanilla extract for 3 to 4 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and falls from the beaters in a slow ribbon. Fold in the plain flour and baking powder, then the milk, until a smooth, thick batter forms.
In a clean dry bowl, beat the egg whites to soft peaks. Add the remaining caster sugar (about 35 g) and continue beating until the whites are glossy and hold firm peaks when the beater is lifted.
Fold one-third of the beaten whites into the yolk batter to loosen it. Then fold in the remaining whites in two additions, working gently so the batter stays light. Pour into the prepared tin.

Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the sponge is set and springy at the centre, has pulled away from the sides of the tin, and a skewer comes out clean. Leave to cool completely in the tin, at least 1 hour.
Soak the sponge
Whisk together the evaporated milk, condensed milk, and 200 ml of double cream in a jug until combined.

Use a skewer or fork to pierce the top of the cold sponge all over, going right through to the base. Pour the three-milk mixture slowly and evenly over the sponge, pausing to let each addition absorb before adding more. The sponge will absorb all of it, though the process takes a few minutes.
Cover the tin with cling film and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight. The sponge should look evenly saturated with no dry patches remaining.
Top and serve
Shortly before serving, whip the 300 ml of double cream with the icing sugar and vanilla extract until soft peaks form. Spread evenly over the top of the soaked sponge with a palette knife.
Dust lightly with ground cinnamon or arrange sliced strawberries over the top. Serve straight from the tin in portions, cut with a sharp knife.

attrs.problem: Sponge does not absorb all the milk mixture
attrs.avoid: Avoid pouring all the milk mixture on at once.
attrs.fix: Pour the three-milk mixture slowly in stages and give each addition 2 to 3 minutes to absorb before adding more. If any pooling remains at the edges after 10 minutes, tilt the tin gently to redistribute. The refrigeration time completes the absorption.

attrs.problem: Beaten egg whites deflate when folded into the yolk batter
attrs.avoid: Avoid using a circular stirring motion when combining the mixtures.
attrs.fix: Fold with a large spatula using a down-and-around motion, rotating the bowl between strokes. Use the first addition of whites (one-third) to loosen the batter so the remaining whites fold in more easily without losing volume.

attrs.problem: Whipped cream topping is too stiff or grainy
attrs.fix: Stop beating as soon as the cream reaches soft peaks and can just hold a shape when a spoon is dragged across it. Overwhipped cream cannot be rescued. If you go too far, fold in 1 to 2 tablespoons of unwhipped cream to loosen it slightly, though the texture will not be identical to cream whipped to the right stage.

attrs.avoid: Avoid using full quantities of condensed milk if a less sweet result is preferred.
attrs.fix: Reduce the condensed milk to 300 ml and increase the evaporated milk to 500 ml. This gives a soak with more savoury milk depth and less sugar while keeping the same total volume.
